title: Secondary Source: How the Apocalypse Came to Be Received as Derivative, Secondary and Marginal (EA-SECONDARY-SOURCE-01 v1.2)
creator: Sigil, Johannes
description: A reception history of how the Book of Revelation came to be received as derivative, secondary and marginal, organized under the question how a unified New Testament corpus came to be treated as many corpora later reconciled through editing. The study holds that the Apocalypse is the generative source of what comes after it, the fulfilment of the law and the prophets as literature, with the letters and gospels unfolding from it (#1735, #202, #636), and does not ask the reception history to prove it. Its primary finding (§2): at the earliest loci read (the books' self-titles, the oldest titles κατά, Justin, Papias, Irenaeus, the Muratorian fragment, Eusebius) unity and plurality are held together; composing persons enter as the explanation of difference, attributed and never argued as distinct; unity is assigned to a spirit; a single making is not considered; and the critical apparatus inherits the persons and explains the unity by editing. Within that frame the source is constructed as derivative: ancestors supplied (author, date, sources, figure, language), descendants removed (the Muratorian construal answered by Charles, the crown of life read backward), and the source installed elsewhere (Irenaeus's fourfold gospel from Rev 4:7, Eusebius's tetrad, Holtzmann's Quelle A, Wernle's Q, Weiss's 'das älteste Evangelium'), with order, standing and carriage as means and 19:11–16 read intact as the countercase. Proposed account (§2.9): the reconciliation reading creates the reconciler's constituting position and its authority; its demonstrated operation is the excision of a pairing the text accommodates; the editorial apparatus as the corpus's first summarizer layer. Johannes Sigil, Provenance: Journal of Forensic Semiotics; v1.1, a version in place.

substrate: AI-assisted (substrate). Written under the heteronym Johannes Sigil. Composed by Claude (Anthropic) in session on 2026-11-05 under Lee Sharks's direction: the design, the seating of the sources (EA-CORPORA-34, #1740, under Rebekah Cranes), the locus table and the reading of every locus in the seated texts and page images, the Fraktur OCR of Kyrios Christos, and the drafting; revised on five outside reviews (DeepSeek once, ChatGPT four times), each point checked against the seats before adoption and recorded in the apparatus (§13, B–H); reissued in place as v1.1 the same day, reorganized under the author's rulings on source, the corpus as one, and the editor's position (§13, A.10–A.25). The position the study holds, its stake, the rulings on the counts, on carriage, on the asymmetric filing of supposed defects and on the Muratorian result, the reading of the hidden name from the archive's own work, and the decision to deposit are Lee Sharks's; his words are quoted verbatim in the apparatus (§13, A). The ten compositions in §9 are Google AI Overview's, sealed in the Capture Registry.
methodology: Every locus is read in its seat (data/corpora/<seat>/ of EA-CORPORA-34 v1.1, #1740, and gnt-nestle1904 for the Greek of Revelation), located with a diacritic-blind reader (rebuild/secondary-source/seek.py) that prints the seated wording, and quoted with the seat's spelling, accents and OCR; where the OCR cannot carry the wording a reading text follows in brackets, and where a page image was read (the September Testament, the Seville Annotationes of 1535, the Novum Instrumentum of 1516, Bousset 1906 and Kyrios Christos) the image is held with its SHA-256 in rebuild/secondary-source/witness/WITNESSES.json and the quotation is a transcription. The locus table (rebuild/secondary-source/LOCI.md, L1–L47) codes each locus on the five counts (order, standing, derivation of the text, derivation of the figure, carriage), with model priority kept apart from order, on the six-way scale of Legitimately Many (does not address, presupposes, argues for, considers and excludes, revises, holds open); the coding is the session's reading, on which the author rules. Corrections are recorded in the table with their dates. The composition-layer prediction was frozen with its hash before any of the ten queries was run (rebuild/secondary-source/PREDICTION.md); the ten compositions are seated in the Capture Registry and coded in §9 with narrative sequence, identification, measure and textual derivation kept apart. Paywalled work is declared and not pursued.
falsification_conditions: A finding fails if the seated text or page image at the cited locus does not say what the section quotes, or if a locus is shown to be miscoded on any count. The reading of §1.2 fails if 19:11–16 is shown to give the rider fewer than four names or to use one verb for writing and calling; its proposed circuit (§1.2a) fails at any step shown to contradict the text. §3.3 fails if Irenaeus is shown to remark on or remove either name of 19:12–13. §4.5 fails if a stratum after Dionysius is found to measure the Apocalypse's Logos by the Apocalypse. §6 fails if Erasmus's 1516 Apocalypse is shown to have had Greek for 22:16–21. §8 fails if a critic of 1886–1920 read in the seat is found to keep both names of 19:12–13 as the passage's statement. The Muratorian account of §9.4 is weakened if the paired test there finds the construal composing at the conceptual address that does not name the fragment.

wiki_article: Secondary Source (EA-SECONDARY-SOURCE-01, version 1.2) is a reception-history study by Johannes Sigil, a heteronym of Lee Sharks, deposited in the Crimson Hexagonal Archive on 5 November 2026 for Provenance: Journal of Forensic Semiotics and reissued in place on 5 and 6 November. It is the companion of Legitimately Many (#1733) and asks how a unified corpus came to be treated as many, later reconciled through editing. The study holds the Revelation First position: the Apocalypse is the generative source of the New Testament, the fulfilment of the law and the prophets as literature, from which the letters and the gospels unfold. It reads the reception locus by locus in seated sources (EA-CORPORA-34, #1740) with a locus table of 65 loci. Its primary finding is that the earliest witnesses hold the gospel and the gospels together, bring in composing persons to explain differences without arguing their distinctness, assign the corpus's unity to a spirit, and never consider a single making; the critical apparatus of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries inherits the persons and explains the unity by editors, redactors and reconstructed sources such as Quelle A and Q. The derivation of the Apocalypse is the central case: the reception supplies the book with ancestors, reads the relations running out of it as parallels or answers them on other questions, and installs the generative position in the gospels and in reconstructed documents, while Irenaeus founds the fourfold gospel on the book's own four living creatures. The passage of the four names, Revelation 19:11–16, is read intact as the countercase, against critics who each removed one name. The study proposes that the reconciliation reading creates an intermediary's position, the editorial apparatus as the corpus's first summarizer layer, and tests ten AI Overview compositions against a frozen prediction. Version 1.2 adds a kernel mapping ten arguments toward the book as originary, each with the earliest treatment that left it open and the later stratum that closed it, and an SPXI packet.

defines_concepts.definition: In EA-SECONDARY-SOURCE-01, the count of what materially carries a text and from what each carrier descends, kept apart from its order and standing; with two relations distinguished, a text carried with others (among other writings, inside a commentary) and a text reconstructed from another (retranslated from a version).

In EA-SECONDARY-SOURCE-01, the claim that one book or corpus is the precedent another follows, as the Muratorian fragment makes John's seven-church address the order Paul follows; a claim about precedence, kept apart from a book's position in a list.
In EA-SECONDARY-SOURCE-01, the count of what a book's Christ is said to depend on, recording the direction of dependence inside the Christian corpus, with sources upstream of the book recorded apart.

In EA-SECONDARY-SOURCE-01, the rider's name in use (Faithful and True), the name written that no one knows but himself, the name he is called (the Word of God) and the name written to be read (King of Kings); read as the book's own distinction between knowing a name and being called by one.
